title: Old Elam
subtitle: 3,200–1,500 BC · Awan, Shimashki and the Sukkalmah

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Awan, the Shimashki kings, and the Sukkalmah's shared kingship

entries.label: The Awan Dynasty and the Treaty with Akkad
entries.hint: Known chiefly from the Sumerian King List and a treaty with Naram-Sin of Akkad, the Awan kings ruled a Susa-centred Elamite state contemporary with Sargon's Akkadian empire — one of the earliest Elamite dynasties documented well enough to be dated and sequenced, even where most individual kings remain little more than names.
entries.note: Sumerian King List, Awan dynasty section; the Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre.

entries.label: Puzur-Inshushinak — the Conqueror King
entries.hint: The last and most powerful Awan king, Puzur-Inshushinak briefly conquered large parts of southern Mesopotamia during Akkad's collapse, leaving royal inscriptions in both Akkadian and the newly invented Linear Elamite script — before Ur-Nammu of the rising Third Dynasty of Ur reversed his conquests entirely.
entries.note: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, Louvre and National Museum of Iran.

entries.label: The Shimashki Dynasty and the Sack of Ur
entries.hint: Succeeding Awan, the Shimashki kings are known largely through their culminating achievement: Kindattu's army sacked Ur in 2004 BC, capturing King Ibbi-Sin and ending the Third Dynasty of Ur — the single most consequential Elamite military success against Mesopotamia in the entire Bronze Age.
entries.note: The Lament for Ur (Sumerian literary text); Elamite king list traditions preserved in later Mesopotamian sources.

entries.label: The Sukkalmah — Shared Kingship
entries.hint: The long Sukkalmah (or Epartid) period governed Elam through a distinctive triarchic system — a sukkalmah ('grand regent') at Susa, a sukkal of Elam and Shimashki, and a sukkal of Susa itself, typically an uncle, nephew and brother — an institutionalised power-sharing arrangement with no real parallel in contemporary Mesopotamian kingship.
entries.note: Sukkalmah-period administrative and legal tablets from Susa; Walther Hinz, 'The Elamite Sukkalmah Period,' Cambridge Ancient History.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The treaty with Akkad, the sack of Ur, and the wars with Babylon

entries.label: The Naram-Sin Treaty Ends a War
entries.hint: The treaty between Naram-Sin of Akkad and an Elamite king, sworn by both the Mesopotamian and Elamite pantheons, formally ended a period of conflict between the two powers and bound the Elamite ruler as a subordinate ally — the occasion for the oldest surviving connected text written in the Elamite language.
entries.note: Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre Sb 8833.

entries.label: Puzur-Inshushinak's Mesopotamian Campaigns
entries.hint: Exploiting the Akkadian Empire's collapse, Puzur-Inshushinak's inscriptions claim conquests reaching well into southern Mesopotamia — a high-water mark of Elamite military reach that proved as short-lived as the Akkadian power vacuum that had made it possible.
entries.note: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, on his claimed conquests.

entries.label: Kindattu Sacks Ur
entries.hint: An Elamite army under Kindattu, joined by forces from Shimashki's allies, stormed Ur and carried King Ibbi-Sin into captivity in Elam — an event Sumerian scribes mourned for generations afterward in the 'Lament for the Destruction of Sumer and Ur,' ending the Third Dynasty of Ur and one of Mesopotamia's great imperial revivals.
entries.note: The Lament for Ur; Sumerian King List, on the end of the Ur III dynasty.

entries.label: Hammurabi Defeats an Elamite-Led Coalition
entries.hint: Hammurabi's own year-names record a decisive victory over an alliance including Elam, Assyria and other regional powers — a reversal of the earlier alliance in which an Elamite-backed coalition had helped Hammurabi's Babylon against Larsa, showing how quickly the era's shifting alignments could turn former allies into declared enemies.
entries.note: Hammurabi's year-name list, on the defeat of the Elamite coalition.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Triarchic succession and the dual Akkadian-Elamite administration

entries.label: Dual Akkadian-Elamite Administration
entries.hint: Susa's administrative and legal tablets from this period were written in both Akkadian and Elamite, sometimes within the same archive, reflecting a genuinely bilingual bureaucratic culture at the crossroads of the Elamite highlands and the Mesopotamian lowland tradition Susa had long been in contact with.
entries.note: Susa administrative and legal tablet corpus, Louvre and National Museum of Iran.

entries.label: Triarchic Succession
entries.hint: Sukkalmah-period succession passed kingship laterally — typically from brother to brother before descending to the next generation's eldest nephew — rather than directly from father to son, a deliberate system that kept power within a wide circle of the royal family and may have reduced (without eliminating) succession disputes common under strict primogeniture.
entries.note: Walther Hinz, 'The Elamite Sukkalmah Period,' Cambridge Ancient History, on the succession pattern reconstructed from dated tablets.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Inshushinak, god of Susa, and the religion of a Bronze Age kingdom

entries.label: Inshushinak, God of Susa
entries.hint: Puzur-Inshushinak's own name — 'servant of Inshushinak' — reflects the central place of Susa's patron deity in Elamite royal ideology from this early period onward; Inshushinak would remain the presiding god of Susa and a figure in Elamite royal titulature for the next fifteen centuries.
entries.note: Puzur-Inshushinak royal inscriptions, invoking Inshushinak.

entries.label: Royal Dedications at the Susa Temples
entries.hint: Sukkalmah-era rulers recorded temple construction and dedication in their own royal inscriptions, continuing a pattern of kings legitimating their rule partly through visible religious patronage — the same basic logic of temple-building kingship attested across contemporary Mesopotamia, expressed in Elam's own religious idiom.
entries.note: Sukkalmah-period royal building inscriptions, Susa.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Royal inscriptions and seals of the Awan and Sukkalmah courts

entries.label: Puzur-Inshushinak's Bilingual Stelae
entries.hint: Puzur-Inshushinak commissioned stone stelae and statues carrying parallel Akkadian and Linear Elamite inscriptions — the two scripts placed side by side as a deliberate statement of a king who ruled, and wished to be read, in both the Mesopotamian and Elamite worlds at once.
entries.note: Puzur-Inshushinak stelae, Louvre Sb 17 and related pieces.

entries.label: Sukkalmah-Era Cylinder Seals
entries.hint: Cylinder seals from Sukkalmah-period Susa show a distinctive local glyptic style — presentation scenes and geometric motifs adapted from, but visibly distinct from, contemporary Old Babylonian seal-cutting conventions — evidence of Elamite artisans absorbing Mesopotamian technique while maintaining a recognisably separate visual tradition.
entries.note: Susa cylinder seal corpus, Louvre Museum; Pierre Amiet, Glyptique susienne (1972).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Linear Elamite script and the oldest Elamite-language text

entries.label: The Oldest Elamite-Language Text
entries.hint: The Naram-Sin–Elam treaty is the oldest known connected text written in the Elamite language, recorded in Akkadian cuneiform script — a linguistic milestone that lets historians confirm Elamite as a genuine, grammatically distinct language centuries before any Elamite-script text of comparable length survives.
entries.note: Naram-Sin–Elam treaty tablet, Louvre Sb 8833; François Vallat, on the treaty's Elamite-language sections.

entries.label: Linear Elamite Script
entries.hint: Puzur-Inshushinak's inscriptions use Linear Elamite, a script distinct from both the earlier undeciphered proto-Elamite and Mesopotamian cuneiform, in use for barely a generation or two before falling out of use entirely — a 2022 collaborative decipherment finally made the script's roughly twenty signs and underlying Elamite readable after a century of failed attempts.
entries.note: François Desset et al., 'The Decipherment of Linear Elamite Writing,' Zeitschrift für Assyriologie (2022).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Tin, lapis lazuli, and Susa's place on the Bronze Age routes

entries.label: Zagros Metal Ores and Susa's Wealth
entries.hint: The Zagros mountains held silver, lead and copper ore deposits Mesopotamia's alluvial plain entirely lacked, giving Elam's economy a metal-producing base that Sumerian and Akkadian cities depended on importing — a structural economic advantage underlying Elam's persistent political relevance across the whole Bronze Age.
entries.note: Zagros mining archaeology; comparative Mesopotamian textual evidence for imported metal dependency.

entries.label: Tin and Lapis Lazuli through Elam
entries.hint: Elam's highland territory straddled the overland routes bringing tin from Central Asia and lapis lazuli from Badakhshan toward Mesopotamia, both essential to Bronze Age craft and prestige economies — control of this transit trade gave Elam consistent economic leverage over its lowland Mesopotamian neighbours regardless of who held the military advantage in any given decade.
entries.note: Comparative sourcing studies of Bronze Age tin and lapis lazuli trade routes through the Iranian plateau.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Bronze metallurgy and the fortification of Susa

entries.label: Bronze Metallurgy at Susa
entries.hint: Direct access to Zagros copper and the tin trade routes passing through Elamite territory let Susa's smiths produce bronze tools and weapons at a scale and consistency that gave Elamite armies and craft production a real material advantage over metal-poor rivals further down the Mesopotamian plain.
entries.note: Metallurgical analysis of Susa bronze artefact assemblages.

entries.label: The Fortification of Susa
entries.hint: Sukkalmah-period Susa was enclosed within substantial defensive walls, reflecting a capital that needed to withstand both Mesopotamian counter-attacks and challenges from rival Elamite power centres on the plateau, such as Anshan, during a period when the dynasty's authority was real but not absolute.
entries.note: Susa excavation reports, on Sukkalmah-period fortification remains.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Treaties, marriage alliances and trade with Akkad and Babylon

entries.label: Royal Marriage Alliances with Ur
entries.hint: Ur III kings gave royal daughters in marriage to Elamite rulers as part of a diplomatic strategy to manage the relationship with their powerful eastern neighbour — a policy that ultimately failed to prevent Kindattu's sack of Ur but demonstrates how seriously Mesopotamian kings took Elam as a diplomatic, not merely military, problem.
entries.note: Ur III royal correspondence and year-name evidence for Elamite marriage alliances.

entries.label: The Susa–Anshan Highland Corridor
entries.hint: The route connecting lowland Susa to the highland city of Anshan in Fars, and onward toward Central Asia, functioned as Elam's own internal backbone as much as an external trade route — the two-centre geography of lowland Susa and highland Anshan would remain a defining structural feature of Elamite political organisation for its entire history.
entries.note: Comparative settlement and trade-route studies linking Susa and Anshan (Tal-e Malyan).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Elam as one of the great Bronze Age powers of the Near East

entries.label: Elam among the Great Bronze Age Powers
entries.hint: Across this entire period Elam stood alongside Akkad, Ur and the Old Babylonian kingdom as one of the handful of states capable of shaping Near Eastern politics at the largest scale — sacking Ur outright, fielding coalition armies, and controlling trade routes no Mesopotamian power could bypass.
entries.note: Comparative Bronze Age political history, Elam and its Mesopotamian contemporaries.

entries.label: The End of the Sukkalmah Order
entries.hint: The Sukkalmah system's triarchic power-sharing gradually gave way around 1500 BC to more conventional father-to-son kingship under the rulers who would found the Middle Elamite kingdom — a transition in the mechanics of succession as significant, in its own way, as any single battle in this folio.
entries.note: Elamite king-list reconstructions, on the Sukkalmah-to-Middle-Elamite transition.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Royal women and an unusual system of succession

entries.label: Royal Women in the Marriage-Alliance System
entries.hint: Princesses married across the Elamite-Mesopotamian frontier functioned as living diplomatic instruments, their marriages recorded in royal correspondence and year-names precisely because the alliances they embodied mattered to the states involved — political agency exercised through kinship rather than through any office the women held in their own right.
entries.note: Ur III royal correspondence and year-name evidence for Elamite marriage alliances.

entries.label: Corvée Labour and the Building of Susa
entries.hint: Sukkalmah-period Susa's fortifications and temple construction, like comparable Mesopotamian building projects of the era, almost certainly depended on conscripted corvée labour drawn from the general population — a form of compulsory service the surviving administrative tablets record in terms of labour-quotas rather than individual experience.
entries.note: Comparative Bronze Age Near Eastern corvée labour practice, inferred from Susa's administrative tablet corpus.
